analysis.one_liner: Expands earned income tax credits for working families, adds Medicare preventive coverage, and funds coal miners' retiree health care through industry premiums.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee reported the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but six days later the Senate set it aside indefinitely by unanimous consent, and it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the earned income tax credit for low-wage families with children, add flu shots, tetanus-diphtheria boosters, and preventive checkups for young children to Medicare, and create a government corporation that guarantees health benefits to retired coal miners whose former employers have disappeared — financed by premiums on coal producers and importers. It would also raise the tax on ozone-depleting chemicals and take away the corporate tax deduction for any executive's pay above $1 million. The Senate Finance Committee wrote and reported the bill, put it on the calendar, and then the whole Senate shelved it by unanimous consent without ever debating or voting on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage working parents with children, through a larger earned income tax credit (the credit percentage for a family with two or more children would rise to 26.75%); Medicare enrollees, who would gain coverage of flu vaccines, tetanus-diphtheria boosters, and well-child services for enrollees under age 7; retired coal miners and their spouses and dependents left without benefits when their employers exited the industry, who would be covered by a new federal corporation; and taxpayers generally, in that companies could no longer deduct executive pay above $1 million as a business expense.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage families, coal retirees, Medicare enrollees

how_it_helps.text: The earned income tax credit would rise to 26.75% of earnings for families with two or more children and 23% for families with one child, phased in over 1992-1994, and the credit would no longer be reduced by interaction with the medical expense deduction or the self-employed health insurance deduction.

Medicare would begin covering influenza vaccines, tetanus-diphtheria boosters, and well-child services (routine visits, immunizations, lab tests, and preventive dental care) for enrollees under age 7.

A new Coal Industry Retiree Health Benefit Corporation would guarantee medical and death benefits to 'orphan' coal miners — retirees whose employers have left the industry — funded by premiums on coal producers and importers rather than by general taxes.

Companies would lose the business tax deduction for any covered officer's annual remuneration above $1 million, so ordinary taxpayers would no longer subsidize that portion of executive pay through the tax code.

The base tax on ozone-depleting chemicals would climb from $1.85 in 1992 to $4.55 by 1995, and the different rates for newly listed chemicals would end, discouraging use of chemicals that damage the ozone layer.

analysis.who_pays: Bituminous coal producers, who would owe 99 cents per hour worked in eastern mines and 15 cents in western mines plus annual per-beneficiary premiums, and coal importers, who would owe 25 cents per ton; companies paying executives more than $1 million, which would lose the deduction for the excess; producers and users of ozone-depleting chemicals, who would pay steadily higher excise taxes that could be passed into prices of refrigeration and foam products; and Medicare beneficiaries, whose monthly premiums would rise slightly (for example, from $36.60 to $36.70) to finance the new benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal producers, chemical makers, high-pay corporations

drawbacks.text: Coal producers and importers would bear new premium obligations per hour worked and per ton imported, and the chemical excise tax would rise sharply through 1995 — costs that producers could pass on to consumers in the prices of energy, refrigeration, and foam products.
Medicare's new preventive benefits would be financed by higher monthly premiums paid by beneficiaries themselves, including a 10-cent-per-month surcharge in 1996 and 1997.

The executive pay limit is a cap on the tax deduction, not on pay itself, so corporations could restructure compensation rather than reduce it; and the coal title obligates 'last signatory' employers and their successor companies to fund retiree benefits, an open-ended liability tied to staying in the coal business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: a bigger paycheck supplement for low-wage parents, preventive care for Medicare enrollees, and a funded guarantee for retired coal miners who did nothing wrong when their employers walked away from promised benefits. The costs fall on identifiable concentrated interests — coal producers, chemical users, and companies with seven-figure executive pay — with some pass-through to consumers. The Medicare premium offset is modest relative to the new benefits. On balance the bill's gains for ordinary people outweigh its costs, though its open-ended employer liabilities in the coal title were the kind of provision industry would fight hard.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate put the bill on its legislative calendar, then a week later set it aside indefinitely by unanimous consent — meaning no senator even objected to shelving it — and it never came up for debate or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate Finance Committee, chaired by the bill's sponsor, ordered an original measure reported on March 3, 1992, and formally reported it to the Senate on March 6 without a written report.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 420, the usual step before floor consideration.
On March 13, 1992, the Senate indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent — a way of setting a bill aside that requires no objection from any senator — and no further action was ever taken.
The bill drew zero cosponsors, so no other senator had publicly attached his or her name to it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers and importers, makers and users of ozone-depleting chemicals, and companies paying executives above $1 million all avoided the bill's new premiums, taxes, and deduction limits. The low-wage families, coal retirees, and Medicare enrollees the bill was written to help gained nothing, since the Senate shelved it without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal producers, chemical makers, big-pay corporations

for.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
for.role: Senate Finance Committee Chairman and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Wrote and introduced the bill as a Finance Committee original measure and reported it to the Senate.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported and placed it on the Senate calendar, putting it in line for floor consideration.

against.name: The United States Senate
against.what_they_did: Indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent on March 13, 1992, one week after it was placed on the calendar, with no senator objecting to shelving it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so no party-line split is visible in the record; the bill was reported by a Democratic chairman and killed by silent unanimous consent rather than by any recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would impose hourly premiums (99 cents eastern, 15 cents western), a 25-cent-per-ton import premium, and per-beneficiary obligations on coal companies to fund retiree health benefits, including for miners abandoned when employers exited. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran directly against retired miners' health coverage.

industries.industry: Producers and users of ozone-depleting chemicals
industries.note: Excise taxes on ozone-depleting chemicals would rise each year through 1995 and rates for newly listed chemicals would equalize, raising costs that could be passed to consumers of refrigeration and foam products.

industries.industry: Corporations paying executives more than $1 million
industries.note: Companies would lose the tax deduction for officer remuneration above $1 million per year, ending a public subsidy of the highest executive pay while leaving the pay itself untouched.

The coal benefits title requires managed care rules — provider networks, drug formularies, Medicare-level physician payments, utilization review — making managed care the permanent delivery channel for coal retiree benefits.

industries.industry: Coal industry retiree benefit plans (1991 Fund)
industries.note: The bill would merge excess assets from closed union-backed plans into a new United Mine Workers of America 1991 Benefit Fund, funded by assessments on last signatory operators, stabilizing benefits for remaining retirees.
